text:
Lynn Conway was a pioneering computer scientist, mathematician, and transgender rights activist born in 1938. After detransitioning from her early attempts at gender transition at MIT in the late 1950s, she pursued a career in electronics and computer architecture at IBM, where she invented multiple-issue out-of-order dynamic instruction scheduling and contributed to the first "superscalar" design. She later joined Xerox PARC in 1973, where she co-founded the multiproject wafers (MPW) technology and co-authored the groundbreaking textbook *Introduction to VLSI Systems* with Carver Mead. Their collaborative work, which introduced scalable, dimensionless design rules and the MOSIS infrastructure for rapid chip prototyping, revolutionized Very Large Scale Integration (VLSI) design, establishing the foundry model that remains central to the semiconductor industry today.
Beyond her technical contributions, Conway is renowned for coining the "Conway effect," which describes how innovations are historically overlooked because their creators do not fit traditional stereotypes of an engineer. She became a prominent advocate for transgender rights, publicly sharing her story in 1999 to raise awareness and protect trans individuals, and was named one of the "Stonewall 40 trans heroes" in 2009. Her legacy includes being inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame in 2023 and receiving numerous accolades, including the IBM Lifetime Achievement Award in 2020 and the IEEE Computer Pioneer Award in 2009. Conway passed away on June 9, 2024, at the age of 86, leaving behind a profound impact on both the technology industry and the fight for gender identity rights.
